location.name: USDA hardiness zone 6a
location.example: Calibrated with Northeast Ohio as the reference point (Summit County). Frost dates and planting windows shift by roughly two weeks for every zone you move.
location.note: Frost dates are averages, not promises — a late frost in the third week of May happens about one year in four in zone 6. Gardening somewhere else? Edit data/garden.json with your own frost dates and the whole calendar follows.
location.howToAdapt: Find your zone at planthardiness.ars.usda.gov, then shift every date in this calendar by about two weeks earlier per warmer zone, or later per colder one.

philosophy: Grow the things that are expensive to buy, taste dramatically better fresh, or produce for months from one planting. Skip the things that are cheap and good at the store. Herbs, cherry tomatoes, greens and garlic clear that bar; onions, potatoes and corn generally do not.

startHere.title: If you grow five things, grow these

items.why: One plant supplies pesto and every tomato dish from July to frost. Store basil is $3 for a handful that dies in two days.
items.how: One plant in a pot by the kitchen door. Pinch flower tips weekly.

items.why: Sungold cherry tomatoes are the variety that converts children into vegetable eaters. Nothing at a store tastes like this.
items.how: One plant in a large pot or bed, caged. Water at the base, never the leaves.

items.why: Produces from June until December in this climate and gets sweeter after frost. It is the last green standing.
items.how: Four transplants in April and four more August 1. Pick outer leaves; the plant keeps going.

items.why: Plant in October, ignore all winter, harvest a year's supply in July. The highest return per minute of work in the garden.
items.how: Break a head into cloves, plant pointy end up 3 inches deep in mid-October, mulch with straw.

items.why: The finishing herb for half the recipes here, and it survives light frost into November.
items.how: Two transplants in May. It is biennial — it will flower and quit in its second spring.

tasks: Order seeds. Read the catalog by the fire; this is the whole point of January.
harvest: Nothing outdoors except stored squash, garlic, potatoes and onions

tasks: Start onion and leek seeds indoors under lights (Feb 1-15).
Start peppers and eggplant indoors March 1-10.
Direct sow spinach, arugula and peas outdoors in the last week if the soil can be worked.
harvest: Overwintered kale, if you mulched it

tasks: Start tomatoes indoors April 1.
Transplant broccoli, cabbage and lettuce outdoors mid-month.
Direct sow carrots, beets, radishes, chard and more spinach.
Plant seed potatoes.
Wait for the frost date. Transplant tomatoes, peppers, eggplant and basil after May 20.
Direct sow beans, cucumbers, zucchini and squash after May 20.
Plant sweet potato slips at the end of the month.
Mulch everything. Stake tomatoes before they need it.
Succession sow beans and cilantro.
Harvest garlic when the lower third of the leaves brown; cure it in a dry shaded place for two weeks.
Sow fall carrots and beets.
Water deeply twice a week rather than lightly every day.
Transplant fall broccoli, cabbage and kale August 1.
Sow spinach and lettuce for fall at the end of the month.
Preserve: freeze roasted tomatoes and pesto in ice cube trays.
Let peppers turn red on the plant — they double in sweetness.
Plant garlic beds' soil amendments now.
Plant garlic mid-month and mulch it with straw.
Cure winter squash in a warm room for 10 days before storing cool.
Bring the rosemary pot indoors before the first hard frost.
Mulch the kale and it will feed you through December.
Clean and oil tools.
Nothing. Rest.
harvest: Kale under snow, if you mulched

containerOnly.note: Mint should only ever be grown in a pot — in a bed it takes the whole bed in two seasons.

localSources.name: Your local farmers market
localSources.note: Herbs, tomatoes, sweet corn and eggs are usually where a market beats a supermarket outright. Go early.

localSources.name: Pick-your-own orchards and berry farms
localSources.when: Strawberries in June, blueberries in July, apples in September
localSources.note: Worth building a weekend around, and the freezer payoff lasts all winter.

localSources.name: Roadside sweet corn
localSources.note: Corn picked that morning is genuinely a different vegetable from what a supermarket sells in March.

localSources.name: Local maple syrup or honey
localSources.when: Maple in late winter, honey in late summer
localSources.note: Both keep for a year and both are a real upgrade over the supermarket version.
